Academic calendar

Winter semester: early January to end of April


Courses and credits

To obtain your 60 ECTS, you will have to validate 12 local credits during your semester abroad.

  • 1st semester (September - December): full-time 4-month internship (20 ECTS) + take part in additional online activities (10 ECTS). Please start your internship research as soon as possible.
  • 2nd semester (January - end of April): you will have to take 12 local credits in order to validate the 30 ECTS remaining.



See below the courses validates by Epitech:


  • Introduction to Programming with Python

An introduction to problem-solving techniques using Python. This course will introduce fundamental programming principles and topics: data types, expressions, control structures, elementary data structures, functions, files, and the mechanics of running, testing and debugging. These concepts will be applied to problem solving and applications in data analysis.

***Prerequisite: Foundations of Mathematics 30, Precalculus 20, Math B30, Math C30, or PMTH 092.

*** *Note: Students may receive credit for one of CS 165 or STAT 165.*


  • Introduction to Digital Systems

Hardware paradigms, logic minimization, sequential and combinational circuits, register transfer notation. Numerical data representation, number bases, floating-point and two’s-complement representation, representation of non-numeric data, records and arrays. Von Neumann architecture, control units, instruction sets, assembly language programming, addressing modes, subroutines, basic building blocks, computer components


  • Java Programming and Applications

Learn to program in the Java programming language. Topics will include the basic building blocks of procedural programming, object-oriented programming, event-oriented programming, graphical user interfaces, simple data structures including arrays and linked lists, and advanced topic including recursion and threads. Problems will be drawn from various science and engineering disciplines. 


  • Introduction to Multimedia Systems

Multimedia is the use of computers to integrate texts, graphics, video, animation, and sound in an interactive experience. The course introduces these elements of multimedia and their associated technologies. Students will gain an appreciation of each element and be able to combine them into a finished work.


  • Building Interactive Gadgets

An introduction to building and controlling interactive devices for multimedia art and DIY projects. Build robots, new musical instruments, wearable computers and more. Learn about sensots and actuators: WiFi, Bluetooth, GPS; hardware platforms such as the Arduino; and software platforms such as Processing and MaxMSP.


  • Data Structures and Abstractions

This course introduces data abstraction, data structures and their implementations, the basics of algorithmic analysis, and the fundamental computing algorithms. Topics include stacks, queues, heaps, recursion, Master Theorem, asymptotic notation, computational complexity, empirical performance measurement, recursion based sorting algorithms, hashing, and trees (including binary trees, B-trees, and AVL trees).

 

  • Web and Database Programming

This course shows how interactive database-driven web applications are designed and implemented. Appropriate protocols and languages for web and database programming will be discussed, with a focus on client-server architectures, interface design, graphics and visualization, event-driven programming, information management, data modeling, and database systems.


  • Methods in Numerical Analysis

Topics will include number systems and errors, solutions of polynomial and other nonlinear equations, interpolation, numerical differentiation and integration, and the cubic spline.


  • Introduction to Data Science

This course introduces data science including current programming languages and libraries for performing data analysis. Topics include data exploration and preparation, data visualization and presentation, computing with data, and an introduction to data modeling and predictive analysis. Technical and communication skills used by data scientists will be introduced. 


  • Risk and Reward in the Information Society

Social context of computing. Case study: human-computer interfaces and their evaluation. Methods and tools of analysis. Professional and ethical responsibilities. Risks and liabilities of computer-based systems. Intellectual property, privacy and civil liberties. Professional communication. Sustainability. Cybercrime.


  • Intro to Digital Multimedia

This course will focus on digital graphic and website design students will learn industry standard and motion graphic software packages: Adobe Photoshop & Premiere, Flash MX, Dreamweaver MX. Students will participate in problem-solving environment using timelines. Projects will require good design concepts and an understanding of multimedia software packages. 


  • Java Programming Language

Introduction to Java (based on an instructor-led Sun course offered in industry). The course covers topics such as arrays, exceptions, GUI interfaces, GUI event handling, Threads, I/O streams and Networking. 


  • Topics in Societal and Ethical Considerations

This course will involve exploration of various considerations of computerized society and what it means to be a professional therein. The student will examine the history of computing, the history of the computing profession, Ethics of professional conduct, intellectual property, and computer crime, among other topics of interest. 


  • Computer Technology for Live Performance

Exploration of the way computer technology can impact various aspects of the performing arts (specifically live theatre, dance, and concert environments for the performing arts (specifically live theatre, dance, and concert environments) including lighting, sound, props and set design as well as projection mapping, virtual/augmented reality, and interactive performance.


  • Topics in Data Acquisition and Analysis

Introduced to data collection techniques by developing their own sensor modules, running experiments and verifying the results. Students will learn microcontroller programming for data collection as well as regression techniques and error analysis for calibration and verification. Potential modules developed range from simple light sensors to fully functioning geiger counters.


  • Introductory Topics in Artificial Intelligence

A course in special topics in which the student makes an independent study in Artificial Intelligence at the second-year level under the supervision of a faculty member in the department.


  • Introduction to Computer Graphics

Introduction to graphics hardware and software. Two-dimensional graphics rendering algorithms. Basic three-dimensional modeling, transformations, viewing geometry, lighting and shading, hidden surface removel, and texture mapping. 


  • Introduction to Artificial Intelligence

Foundations and main methods of Artificial Intelligence. Problem characteristics and spaces. Search and optimization techniques with a focus on uninformed and heuristic algorithms. Two player games and constraint satisfaction. Modelling and simulation. Comparison of logic-based, fuzzy, and probabilistic reasoning and knowledge representation methodologies. Machine learning: learning tasks, inductive learning, statistical-based learning, over-fitting, accuracy. 


  • Introduction to Operating Systems

Overview of operating systems: functionality, and design issues. Operating system principles: structures, abstractions, APIs, resource allocation, proximity, virtualization. Concurrency: process state, context switches, process communication, synchronization. Scheduling: preemption, schedulers, processes, and threads. Memory management. Security and protection. File systems. User interface. Distributed algorithms: consensus, termination, and fault tolerance. 


  • Computer Networks

Network architectures and protocols, networked applications, reliable data delivery, routing and forwarding, local area networks, resource allocation, mobility, reliability through redundancy. Security: secure design, defensive programming, threats and attacks, network security, cryptography. 


  • Advanced Data Structures and Algorithm Design

Fundamental algorithms: depth- and breadth-first traversals, pattern matching, and graph algorithms. Algorithmic strategies: brute-force, greedy, divide-and-conquer, backtracking, branch-and-bound, dynamic programming, and randomized. Algorithm analysis, complexity theory, performance evaluation. Parallelism: fundamentals, algorithms, communication. 


  • Programming Language Concepts

Programming language genealogy and design. Imperative, functional, and object-oriented language paradigms. Context-free grammars and syntax trees. Data types, control structures, exception handling, data abstraction, information hiding, and non-determinism. Program representation, translation, and execution. Functional programming: advantages, constructs, closures, and higher-order operations. Parallel programming. *


  • Numerical and Symbolic Computing

Least squares and other approximations. Difference equations. Solutions of algebraic systems. Symbol manipulators.


  • Data Wrangling

Introduction to the fundamentals of data wrangling including processes of data acquisition, integration, transformation, and cleaning throughout the data life cycle. Emphasis on the importance of data quality with topics in data integrity, security, and social responsibility. Techniques for effective visualization and communication through project work. 


  • Database and Information Retrieval

Information management: concepts and applications. Motivation for database systems. Components of database systems. Data modeling: conceptual, spreadsheet, relational, object-oriented, and semi-structured models. Querying and database query languages. Caching and transaction processing. Other topics include distributed databases, physical database design, and information retrieval systems.


  • Web Content Development and Production

Explore various leading-edge technologies for digital multimedia content creation and production for web-based delivery. Examine issues for media conversion and compression, and their effect on communication. Students will demonstrate these ideas in a web-based project.


  • User Interface Implementation and Evaluation

User Interfaces are an essential part of any interactive software application. Ideally. the interface will accommodate users from beginners to experts by providing a low threshold and a high ceiling to interactions with the software. Students will implement a user interface with existing tool kits and then evaluate their interface with users.


  • Mobile Computing

Developing software applications (called apps) for mobile computing platforms such as smart phones, tablets and personal media devices. Topics may include touch-screen interfaces, power management, graphics optimization, communication, location, and mobile browsers. App marketplaces and network carrier policies will also be discussed. For each term, the course will concentrate on a single platform, such as iOS, Android, or Windows Phone 7, and culminate in a large-scale project.


  • Special Topics in Virtual Reality

Introductory topics in virtual reality. Environments, Platforms, Locomotion, Physiology, Applications.


  • Intermediate Topics in Artificial Intelligence

A course in special topics in which the student makes an independent study in Artificial Intelligence at the third-year level under the supervision of a faculty member in the department.


  • Advanced Digital Systems Architecture

Advances in computer architecture. Topics will be selected from performance enhancements, digital signal processing architectures, architectures for networks and distributed systems, architectures for mobile devices, and recently proposed architectures. 


  • Computer Graphics

Advanced topics in computer graphics, including special modeling techniques for natural phenomenon, advanced illumination models and rendering algorithms.


  • Animation Software Design

This course teaches the design and implementation of software for creating animations. Topics include history of animation, technical background, motion control, keyframe-based animation, kinematics, physically based animation, fluid animation, modelling and animating human figures, facial animation, modelling behavior, and special models for animation.


  • Interactive Entertainment Software

This course teaches the design and implementation of interactive entertainment software, including computer games. Topics include history of interactive software, social factors, principles of interactive entertainment, hardware platforms, current software development tools, game design, game architecture, game physics, collision detection, game graphics, artificial intelligence for games, audio, game production and business aspects.


  • Computability and Formal Languages

The notion of effective procedure and Turing machine. The universal Turing machine. Nondeterministic Turing machine. Recursive functions and other computable functions. The halting problem and unsolvability. Grammar and formal language. Finite automata and regular grammars. Context-free grammars and push-down automata. Post correspondence problem. The Chomsky hierarchy of languages and context-sensitive language.


  • Advanced Artificial Intelligence

Advanced Artificial Intelligence approaches to approximate reasoning and machine learning. Decision trees and other selected data-based knowledge models. Topics may include logic programming and PROLOG, LISP, Artificial Intelligence in games, data mining, natural language processing, pattern recognition, and planning.


  • Image Processing

Introduction to image processing systems. Image transformation. Image enhancement. Image coding and compression. Feature extraction and image segmentation.

Introduction to Computer Audio

The purpose of this course is to provide a broad overview of many areas of computer audio, including: Digital representation and compression; Psychoacoustics; Surround Sound; Speech recognition and Music Information Retrieval; MIDI and New interfaces for music; and video game sound. We will also explore modular interactive software environments such as Max/MSP and PD.


  • Human Computer Communications

This course stresses the importance of good interfaces and the relationship of user interface design to human-computer interaction. Other topics include: interface quality and methods of evaluation; interface design examples; dimensions of interface variability; dialogue genre; dialogue tools and techniques; user-centered design and task analysis; prototyping and the iterative design cycle; user interface implementation; prototyping tools and environments; I/O devices; basic computer graphics; color and sound.


  • Advanced Topics in Operating Systems

Advanced operating system concepts. Topics include one or more of the following: distributed systems, real-time operating systems, intelligent networks, communications protocols, and database process control within a client-server framework.


  • Cryptography and Network Security

Classical cryptosystems, data encryption standards, advanced encryption algorithms, public key cryptosystems, digital signatures, IP security, and web security.


  • Information Visualization

Focuses on design, development, and study of interactive visualization techniques for the analysis, exploration, and explanation of abstract information. Topics covered: principles of visual perception, information data types, visual encodings of data, representations of relationships, interaction methods, evaluation techniques. 


  • Mobile Computing

Mobile Computing focuses on the design and implementation of software in a networked mobile environment. The primary topics to be covered in the course include software development practices, network computing, graphics programming, and human-computer interaction, all focused on the challenges and opportunities afforded by modern mobile computing devices.


  • Virtual and Augmented Reality

Design and implementation of software in virtual and augmented reality environments. Development practices, assets and avatars, interaction, locomotion, psychological effects, audio, multiplayer considerations, applications. Limitations and future developments. 


  • Advanced Topics in Numerical Analysis

Numerical solutions of ordinary differential equations. Numerical solutions of partial differential equations. Linear and non-linear problems. 


  • Data Mining

Knowledge Discovery from Data (KDD). Topics include knowledge discovery, data preparation, data warehousing, pattern mining, classification and regression, cluster analysis, outlier detection, mining complex data types.


  • Management Support Systems

Strategic and tactical rewards resulting from the effective use of corporate information systems will be presented. Topics include techniques and tools for developing management support systems. Case studies on development and use of the systems will be discussed.


  • Advanced Topics in Database Systems

Advanced database systems concepts. Topics include one or more of the following: in-depth study of topics covered in CS 375; inclusion dependency and semantic data models; object-oriented databases; probabilistic databases; Web databases; data mining.


  • Software Development Project

Software development projects following all the phases of the software process. Project planning and scheduling. Surveys on architectural styles, design patterns and components. Semester-long group projects with real-world applications. Projects will be integrative, require evaluation of potential solutions, and require work on a larger scale than typical course projects.


  • Special Topics: Computer Graph

Special topics in computer graphics: 3D viewing transformation and perspective projection, ray-tracing and radiosity rendering techniques, multiresuolution surface models, special advanced modelling techniques.


  • Emerging User Interface Design

Discover new and emerging principles of UI design. Derive guidelines directly applicable to industrial applications from research in the fields of Psychology, HCI, and Software Engineering Methodologies. 


  • Adv. Obj. Oriented Prog.in C++

The student will investigate topics related to object oriented programming in C++ and will implement a class hierarchy for several data structures and algorithms. As well, the student will develop several demonstration applications to illustrate the use of the class hierarchy.


  • Topics in Data Comm & Network

Topics in Data Communications and Networks: Protocol Concepts, Local Area Networking, Wide Area Networking, Network Programming. 


  • Designing Animation With Flash

Learning the basics of multimedia animation design. Learning how to use Macromedia's Flash software.


  • Soc. &Eth. Impl. of Computing

To study the social and ethical implications of computing and telecommunications. Topics include computerization, quality of life, unemployment, personal privacy and freedom.


  • Natural Language Processing

Natural Language Processing: Principles of Natural Language Processing, Grammars Language Formalisms, Declarative Cause Grammars, Project.


  • Server-side web applications

Students will study the concepts and competing technologies involved in web-based application development and will use JSP, servlets, HTTP, and JDBC in the development of their own server-side applications.


  • Advanced Database Design

Review database schema design using FDs. Examine various methods of using MVDs to design acyclic databases. Investigate why these methods fail when using EMVDs. Examine the use of sematntic models in database schema design.


  • Computer Game Programming

Principles of Computer Games. History. Simulation and Modelling, graphics, artificial intelligence, real-time processing, game theory, and web based games. Project.


  • Applied Image Processing

Study of basic image processing algorithms. Applications of selected techniques to practical problems. A term project is required.


  • Bayesian Networks

Uncertain reasoning. Modeling probabilistic knowledge using directed acyclic graphs. Directed separation and its relationship with probabilistic conditional independence. Inference algorithms for processing queries given evidence.


  • Computer Audio Topics

Representation of audio, compression, spatialization and surround sound, analysis and synthesis, speech, music, temporal and spectral processing. 


  • Principles and Techniques of Augmented Reality and Virtual Reality

In this directed readings course, the goal will be to designan Augmented Reality (AR) application in Unity. The main contribution to the project will be the creation of realistic holograms and the incorporation of objectrecognition using libraries such as OpenCV. Feedback from the users will be an important part in the designing process of the app, as it will influence the decisions made about UI design and the features to be implemented. The app will be tested on a Microsoft HoloLens using its Mixed Reality Toolkit for Unity, or on other devices capable of doing AR if they are found to be more suitable for the users.


  • Open Source Software Development

This course will introduce students to software development in an open source environment, including methodology and philosophy. Students will gain hands-on experience with the tools used in open source development, leading to contributions to an active open source software development project. Students will also have the opportunity to enhance their general programming skills in a very practical way. 


  • Wireless Technologies

Study and analysis of several wireless communications, such as Bluetooth, RFID and Wi-fi-by including case studies.


  • Web Service Design

This course will explore issues around the design, coding, and deployment of web-based services for public use. Topics of study will include various architectures for web-based systems, including their programming. Mash-ups of existing services will also be considered. Students will develop and test a web-based service.


  • Computational Models in Meaning of Music

This course will investigate existing and new models of music analysis, including cognitive, affective, expectational, and self-referential models. Topics will be drawn from pattern recognition, cognitive science, and musicology


  • Foundations and Applications in Data Mining

Foundations and applications of data mining. Topics include one or more of the following: data preparation and transformation, review of relevant quantitive methods, data characterization, generalization, classification and prediction, clustering, association, on-line analytical processing, data warehousing, data analysis, model development, interpretation.


  • Topics in Interactive Entertainment

This course investigates one or more topics in interactive entertainment in depth. Topics may include: game studies, game design, game programming, graphics and animations for games, artificial intelligence for games, game physics, game audio, game production, and recent advances in interactive entertainment.


  • Visual Analytics

Visual analytics is a multi-disciplinary field that facilitates analytical reasoning through interactive visual interfaces. The student will therefore study aspects of visualization, human factors, and data analysis in aid of conducting an analysis of available data.


  • Mobile Application Development and Deployment

Programming for mobile deployment platforms such as smartphones and tablets. Views, models, navigation, interfaces, graphics. Development environments, app stores, cross-platform deployment.


  • Mobile Computing

Mobile Computing focuses on the design and implementation of software in a networked mobile environment. The primary topics to be covered in the course include software development practices, network computing, graphics programming, and human-computer interaction, all focused on the challenges and opportunities afforded by modern mobile computing devices.


  • Information Visualization

Information Visualization focuses on the design, development, and study of interactive visualization techniques for the analysis, comprehension, exploration, and explanation of large collections of abstract information. Topics to be covered include principles of visual perception, information data types, visual encodings of data, representations of relationships, interaction methods, and evaluation techniques

Note: Course lists are given for information only. They can change from year to year. If a course is not available when you arrive on site, EPITECH cannot be held responsible for it.

1. Application

Students should have their application process completed by March 15th. They will then need to have their courses selected by May 1st. The partner University will be the one providing the information throughout the whole process.


The university will most likely ask you for:

  • Official Transcripts in English (stamped & signed by home institution)
  • Passport copy (valid 6 months after the program end date)
  • Proof of Financial Support in English
  • Health Insurance is mandatory


To be given to Epitech bachelor campus administration to reenroll for the Tech4 (in April/May):

  • The addendum to the contract.
  • EPITECH re-registration dossier.

This information is subject to change by the partner university. They will provide you with the most current information upon your acceptance.


2. Visa (more information here)

You can find all the detailed information on the US government website or the Embassy of the US in Paris website.


1/ Admission letter and DS-20 form

When you have been admitted to the university, you will receive an acceptance letter and an DS-20 form, allowing you to apply for the J-1 student visa at the embassy. Please check the information on DS-20 carefully and sign the document.


2/ Pay the SEVIS fees

 You must then pay the SEVIS I-901 fees online (here). Make sure you print the receipts. The fees for students are $350.


3/Complete the DS-160 form

Complete DS-160 form and upload an ID photo meeting the following requirements. Print the application form confirmation page to bring to your interview.

You will have to pay a visa application fee (non refundable) before your interview of $185 (more information here).


4/Schedule an appointment at the consulate

For people in France, you need to make an appointment for your interview at the US Consulate. Plan to travel to Paris for it.

If you live in another country, check the different consulate/embassy.

You can check the deadlines for obtaining an appointment for submitting a file, here.


During your interview at the consulate, you must:

  • have the necessary supporting documents to prove that you qualify for the category of visa that you request--document relating to your current studies and its relationship to the studies you wish to pursue in the United States: academic transcript, various certificates, SAT or TOEFL test scores, diplomas, etc.
  • demonstrate, with supporting evidence, to the consular officer that you have solid family, social and financial ties to France and that you intend to return there once your residence permit has expired.
  • prove that you have the financial means necessary to finance your studies and live in good conditions in the United States for the first 12 months. Any document proving your family or relational ties with any person funding your studies, as well as bank statements, tax notices thereof.

Please note that the visa gives you the right to work 20 hours on campus.


3.Insurance and Health (more information here)

Option 1: insurance through UWG

International students on F1 & J1 visas are automatically enrolled in the United Health Care (UHC) student health insurance plan each Fall and Spring.

Student Annual Cost (Fall, Spring/Summer): $2,936. Cost for Fall 2025: $1,231. Cost for Spring / Summer 2026: $1,705


Option 2: private international insurance

Please note that alternate insurance plans must meet certain requirements. They are reviewed by UHC via their waiver request process each semester. UWG is not involved in the process.


It is imperative that you take out insurance that will cover you for your medical and hospital expenses, repatriation and accompanied by civil liability. International insurance must cover the entire period of your studies in the country. Insurance costs are the responsibility of each student. To take out international insurance, the market is quite open. Please click here for more information.

For more information, you can consult the country’s health file at: https://www.diplomatie.gouv.fr/fr/conseils-aux-voyageurs/conseils-par-pays-destination/etats-unis/

Note: It is advisable to register on the French register established outside France and to report to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs via the Ariane platform: https://pastel.diplomatie.gouv.fr/fildariane/dyn/public/login.html.


4.Prepare your arrival

Read more about the university here.

Check the International Student Checklist provided by the university here.

schools.courses:
Credits

Number of local credits to earn per year for the undergraduate program: 24; 12 per semester (in order to validate 60 ECTS)


Academic calendar

Fall semester: classes start from mid-August and end mid-December

Spring semester: classes begin early January and end mid-May


Department and Courses

The courses validated by EPITECH are the following:


CS-3110 System Architecture

An introduction to systems architecture and its impact on software execution. Topics include digital logic and digital systems, machine level representation of data, assembly level machine organization, memory systems organization, I/O and communication, and CPU implementation.


CS-3201 Program Construction I

The craft and science of software construction: effective practices, principles, and patterns for building correct, understandable, testable and maintainable object-oriented code.


CS-3202 Program Construction II

A continuation of CS 3201: effective practices, principles and patterns for building correct, understandable, testable, and maintainable code using a variety of programming paradigms, programming languages and system architectures.


CS-3270 Intelligent Systems 

Application and survey of problem-solving methods in artificial intelligence with emphasis on heuristic programming, production systems, neural networks, agents, social implications of computing, and professional ethics and responsibilities.


CS-4180 Advanced Web Development

This course focuses on current industry best practices used to develop dynamic, interactive, multi-page websites. Topics include user-interface development, common web components, database interactions, and security.


COMP-3310 Mobile Development

This course introduces the fundamentals in the design, implementation, and distribution of mobile applications. Topics include mobile device architecture, software engineering, user interface design, and app distribution.


COMP-3350 Game Development I

This course introduces the process of the design and development of video games. Topics include game history, game styles, game components, game evaluation and analysis, and game development using a modern game engine and programming language.


COMP-4350 Game Development II

This course introduces more advanced concepts and topics in game development, including 3D game development, using a modern game engine.


COMP-3400 System and Network Administration I

This course covers the fundamentals of network and operating system theory and practice. Topics include the TCP/IP protocol stack, routing, basic OS administration, and basic network services.


COMP-3500 Cybersecurity

This course provides an overview of computer and network security and countermeasure techniques. Topics include cryptography, Public Key Infrastructures (PKI), viruses, malware, security of different layers of the TCP/IP, Firewall, and VPN, TLS, Bitcoin, and Web security. Techniques and tools used in defending network security will also be covered.


COMP-3600 User-Centric Computing I

The course introduces the fundamentals of human computer interaction (HCI) and the principles in the design and evaluation of user interfaces. Topics covered include: guidelines/principles in interface design, usability evaluation, universal design


COMP-3800 Data Analytics

This course introduces the basics of data science and data analytics to extract information from unstructured data. Topics include technologies, techniques, and tools in data collection, storage, processing, and analysis.


COMP-4200Advanced Database Systems

This course introduces the advanced DB topics, such as stored procedures, functions, triggers, indexes, performance tuning and query optimization.


COMP-4300 Application Development II

In this course students will learn and apply effective practices, principles, and patterns of large-scale software development and testing as part of collaborative development teams.


COMP-4420 DevOps

This course provides an introduction to the principles of DevOps and the DevOps tools that enable the optimization of an organization s development workflow. Topics include DevOps concepts, build automation, provisioning, monitoring, and deployment, among others.


CS-4225 Distributed and Cloud Computing

This course introduces the foundations and applications of distributed and cloud computing. Topics include multi-threaded programming, scheduling, synchronization, network architecture, distributed computing and distributed services, cloud services, and internet-scale computing.


CS-4275 Machine Learning Foundations

A broad introduction into the theoretical foundations and essential algorithms for supervised and unsupervised learning with a focus on best practices and real-world problems.


MATH-4873 Advanced Data Analytics

This course introduces computation-intensive statistical approaches and modern machine learning methods. Topics include:1. R-computing and programming (intermediate to advanced)2. Rmarkdown3. Data scraping and text mining4. Random number simulations5. Bootstrapping6. Optimization7. Regression8. Analysis of Variance9. Classification, Clustering10. Network data analysis


MATH-3873 Statistical Programming 

This course helps develop programming skills necessary for statistical analysis and data science. Students will learn the basic syntax and functions of the programming language, data organization and visualization, programming, as well as how to use existing packages of the language. Case studies in applied statistics, data science, or machine learning will be discussed.


Important Notes

  • Presence in class is compulsory, under penalty of loss of visa and repatriation to France at the student's expense (impact on credits).
  • The courses are most likely more academic than at EPITECH.
  • The course list is given for information only. It can change from year to year.
  • If a course is not available when you arrive on site, EPITECH cannot be held responsible for it.,
  • Any Tech 4 abroad involves an EIP! Take advantage of the free slots you will have to advance it.

Application dossier


Once the IAFF office has sent your nomination, the partner university will contact you directly by email to start your application. All required documents will have to be uploaded on their platform or sent by email before the deadline (see EMEA Teams channel for each application deadline).


If you have not received anything yet, it means your nomination has not been sent yet, please be patient.

Visa


For European students, a valid passport/ national ID card is sufficient to travel to Europe (exception for the UK).


For non-Europeans students or students with a non-European citizenship, please check the immigration office of the host country to check the visa process and fees.


Students in France can use this website: https://www.diplomatie.gouv.fr/fr/


Insurance


For European students


The European Health Insurance Card (CEAM in French) is nominative and individual. This card certifies your rights to the Health Insurance in Europe. To obtain your card, log in to your Ameli account at least two months before your departure. It is free of charge and will be sent to your place within two weeks. You can also download it online.


For more information: https://www.ameli.fr/assure/droits-demarches/europe-international/protection-sociale-etranger/etudes-etranger


For non-European students


You must register for a private health insurance to cover your full stay. Please check with your parents, bank, or any private insurance company for more information depending on the wanted coverage.


Please register via the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (Ariane) platform to be aware of any news (terrorist attack, tsunami, earthquake…) in your host country for French citizens only: https://pastel.diplomatie.gouv.fr/fildariane/dyn/public/login.html


Campus life


Erasmus+ students, for the most part, live in the university residence. The dormitory "Varaždin" is a 7 minute walk from the city center and the campus (FACULTY OF ORGANIZATION AND COMPUTER SCIENCE).


You can find pictures here.


The price of a room varies between 100 and 150 euros per month. Single, double or triple rooms are available. They are equipped with beds with mattresses, sheets and bed linen, a desk, chair and drawer, bathroom with toilet, fridge, internet access and TV.


There are also kitchens, living rooms, terraces, work rooms, gym, laundry and bicycle storage.


You can find other solutions for housing here: http://www.unizg.hr/homepage/international-exchange/exchange-students/student-services/housing/

schools.name: Vancouver Island University
schools.overview: Vancouver Island University (VIU) is a public university founded in 1936 and currently has approximately 12,000 students and over 100 different study programs. Small course sizes with a maximum of 34 students create ideal learning conditions and a dynamic exchange between students and lecturers. VIU's main campus is located in the port city of Nanaimo on Vancouver Island on the west coast of Canada. Numerous outdoor activities and sports are possible all year round thanks to the close proximity to the sea, forests and mountains. The metropolis of Vancouver is just a ferry ride away and the popular tourist destination of Victoria is easily accessible by bus.
schools.administrative:
1. Application

To apply to VIU, please submit the following documents via email to their European office:

  • Application form
  • Official academic transcripts in English
  • Master students also need to hand in their Bachelor diploma in English
  • Proof of English proficiency (Tepitech certificate)
  • Valid passport copy

To be given to Epitech bachelor campus administration to reenroll for the Tech4 (in April/May):

  • The addendum to the contract
  • EPITECH re-registration dossier


2. Visa

(See the Americas Teams channel for information or deadline to follow)

Many students who study in Canada for less than six months do not require a Study Permit. Please note that visa-exempt foreign nationals who fly to or transit through Canada will need an Electronic Travel Authorization (eTA). Detailed information is available on the Canadian Embassy’s website


As a student for 1 year, you need to apply ONLINE for a Study Permit which will automatically issue an electronic travel authorization. Vancouver Island University is on the Designated Learning Institution List with the number O19395299688.

https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/study-permit.html


You can follow the application guide

Forms which need to be completed, signed and dated:

  • Application for Study Permit made Outside of Canada (IMM 1294)
  • Family Information (IMM 5707)
  • Authority to Release Personal Information to a Designated Individual (IMM 5475) if applicable
  • Statutory Declaration of Common-Law Union (IMM 5409) if applicable

Other documents:

  • Proof of payment (biometric and Study Permit)
  • Photocopy of passport showing passport number, issuance and expiry dates, photo, name, date and place of birth
  • Two photos meeting visa application photograph specifications
  • Letter of acceptance from your Canadian school
  • Provincial attestation letter / Territorial Attestation Letter
  • Proof of financial support
  • Medical exam
  • Photocopy of marriage license/certificate if applicable
  • Any additional documents required by the responsible visa office


3. Insurance

All VIU students must obtain Canadian health insurance for the entire study period, arranged via VIU.

Further information is available here


4. Scholarship

Every year, Vancouver Island University (VIU) awards three scholarships to students who spend a semester abroad at VIU in Canada and who applied via the European office.

  • Scholarships Canada: Spring Term
  • One partial scholarship awarded to students studying abroad at VIU from January to April: 1 x 1,000 CAD
  • Scholarships Canada: Fall Term
  • Two partial scholarships awarded to students studying abroad at VIU from August to December: 1 x 1,000€ and 1 x 1,000 CAD


Scholarships Canada: Requirements

You are eligible if you:

  • Applied for a study abroad term at VIU at the indicated times
  • Are successfully enrolled in a Bachelor or Master term at VIU through the International Student Office
  • Consent to writing 10 different experience reports during your term (5 in English and 5 in your native language, 400-600 words each, including 3 self-taken photos), or agree to produce 8 short videos (90-180 seconds), or produce 10 Facebook or Instagram posts for social media channels
  • Provide a Curriculum Vitae (CV) with a headshot in English
  • Submit a letter of motivation or video in English (min. 500 words) on the topic: “What to expect from a study abroad period at VIU?”

Send scholarship applications for spring term by November 15 of the previous year, and for fall term by June 15 of the same year via email to your contact person at the International Student Office.

Winners will be notified by mid-December / July via email.

More information here


Campus life

Many activities (mainly outdoors) are available near the university. There are also various student associations to participate in during your exchange.

  • Student life at VIU
  • International student office website
  • Resources for International students
  • Experience reports by VIU students
  • Connect with VIU students via Facebook

schools.courses:
Credits

Students must validate 12 credits per semester (i.e. 24 for the academic year) in order to validate 60 ECTS. Which corresponds to 4 courses (per semester).


Academic Calendar

1st semester: end of August to mid-December

2nd semester: January to April


IMPORTANT:

Presence in class is compulsory, under penalty of loss of visa and repatriation to your home country at the student's expense (impact on credits). The courses are most likely more academic/theoretical than at Epitech.

The course list is given to you for information purposes only. It can change from year to year. If a course is not available when you arrive on site, EPITECH cannot be held responsible.


EIP: Any tech4 abroad involves an EIP! Take advantage of the free slots you will have to advance them.


Courses

You have to take 4 courses per semester (=12 credits)

See below the list of courses validated by Epitech:


  • Topics in Computer Science (3 credits)

An introduction to applied and theoretical topics, designed to develop an understanding of key concepts in computer science. Topics include digital logic, programming language paradigms including logic and functional programming, computer organization and architecture, system software, software engineering principles, and theory of computation.


  • Systems and Networks (3 credits)

An introduction to operating systems and computer networks. Topics include network architectures, communications protocols, client / server architecture and file systems. The lab component includes hardware and software installations, upgrades and backups.


  • Data Structures (4 credits)

An examination of various methods of representing and manipulating data, including internal representation of data, stacks, queues, linked lists, trees and graphs. Analysis of algorithms will also be discussed extensively.


  • Computer Architecture & Assembly Language (3 credits)

An introduction to computer organization, and machine and assembly languages. Topics include data representation, the instruction set and addressing modes of a chosen processor, procedures and parameter passing, and the use of operating system services.


  • Software Engineering (3 credits)

An exploration of the methods and tools for developing high quality software. The course includes topics in program design, program style, algorithm selection, interface design, debugging and testing, system utilities, version control, regular expressions and an introduction to scripting languages. 


  • Introduction to the Practice of Cyber-Security (3 credits)

An introduction to key cyber-security concepts as applied to information systems in a business environment. Topics include assessing risk in cyber-security, attack vectors, tenets of cyber-security, the human element, operation security, application security, mobile and IoT security, and incident response plans. 


  • Introduction to Human-Computer Interaction (3 credits)

An introduction to understanding human behaviour as it applies to interface design, implementation, and evaluation. Topics include: design issues and goals, the limits of the human cognitive system, user-centered design, prototyping, establishing requirements, evaluation techniques, and design implications of emerging technologies.


  • Web Programming (4 credits)

Exploration of languages, tools and techniques to write software for use within the World Wide Web (WWW). The course includes the WWW client/server model and related protocols, web server properties, web markup languages, client/server scripting tools, server side programming, and database access tools.


  • Foundations of Computer Science (3cr)

A survey of formal models and results that form the theoretical foundation of computer science. Typical topics include finite automata, Turing machines, simple undecidable problems, context-free languages, grammars and elementary computational complexity. 


  • Programming Languages (3cr)

The fundamental concepts of imperative and applicative programming languages. Topics include the description of data types, variable assignment and sharing, sequencing, iteration and recursion, parameter passing mechanisms, and type checking. 


  • Object-Oriented Software Development (3 cr)

Topics include aspects of object-oriented analysis, design and development; definition and comparison of object-oriented metrics; verification methods for OO-software; maintenance and reuse issues. 


  • Digital Logic and Computer Organization (4cr)

The fundamentals of logic design, computer organization, and the structure of major hardware components of computers. Topics include the application of Boolean algebra to switching circuits; the use of MSI, LSI and field programmable devices in digital design; combinatorial and sequential circuits, flip flops, counters, memory organization, CAD tools. 


  • Intro to Operating Systems (3cr)

An introduction to the major concepts of operating systems and study of the interrelationships between the operating system and the architecture of computer systems. Topics include operating system structures, concurrent programming techniques, cpu scheduling, deadlocks, memory management, file systems and protection. 


  • Database Systems (3cr)

An introduction to the use and operating principles of database management systems. Topics include data entities and relationships, data modelling using Entity-Relationship Diagrams, hierarchical, network and relational models of databases, query language, physical representation of data in secondary storage, relational algebra and calculus as applied to the design of databases, security and integrity in the context of concurrent use, and basic ethical issues associated with database design and use. 


  • Intro to Systems Analysis (3cr)

The methods and methodologies used in analyzing and designing various types of systems. Topics include project definition, CASE tools, data gathering, structured analysis and design, human-machine interface, database design, system controls, hardware selection and system testing, implementation and operation. Students are assigned to a project team involved in a system study as part of the course. 


  • Computers and Society (3cr)

An introduction to the social, philosophical and ethical issues of technology with an emphasis on computing technology. Topics covered include privacy, social control, information, the changing nature of work and appropriate technology.


  • Computer Graphics (3cr)

The fundamental algorithms and data structures used in generative computer graphics. Topics include structure of interactive graphics programs, raster algorithms, colour, two- and three-dimensional geometric transformations, animation, parallel and perspective projection, hidden line and hidden surface algorithms, cubic curves and surfaces, and shading models. Optional topics include fractals/L-systems, and GPU hardware programming. 


  • Advanced Algorithms (3 cr)

A survey of advanced topics in algorithm design and analysis. Typical topics include complexity analysis, strategies for intractable problems, approximation algorithms, random algorithms, advanced data structures for sorting and searching, graph and network algorithms, amortized analysis. 


  • Advanced Topics in Algorithms and Complexity (3 cr)

This course examines selected emerging and advanced topics in Algorithms and Complexity Theory. Topics may include: advanced techniques for algorithm analysis; complexity classes; algorithmic techniques in graph theory, combinatorics, and optimization; approximation algorithms; distributed and parallel algorithms; probabilistic algorithms; online algorithms; quantum algorithms. May be taken more than once in different topics with permission of Department Chair.


  • Advanced Topics in Programming (3 cr)

This course examines selected emerging and advanced topics in programming. Topics may include: a detailed analysis of language design, semantics, verification, resource utilization, language support for concurrency, meta-programming, and compilers. May be taken more than once in different topics with permission of Department Chair.


  • Networks and Communications (3 cr)

An introduction to computer networks and communications. Topics include local and wide area networks, network architectures, security, communications protocols, routing, and an introduction to distributed computing.


  • Embedded and Real-Time Software Systems (3 cr)

The theory and practice of developing embedded systems with time and resource constraints. Students design, develop and deploy embedded systems on hardware ranging from bare-metal micro-controllers to systems with a real-time OS to Embedded Linux systems. Time-oriented topics include bare-metal programming, cooperative multitasking and preemptive multitasking. 


  • Advanced Topics in Software Engineering (3 cr)

This course examines selected emerging and advanced topics in software engineering. Topics may include: software verification and validation techniques, techniques to model and analyze software processes, software design for various architectures (service-oriented, component-oriented, message-oriented), automation of software delivery pipelines, case studies of large scale software successes and failures. 


  • Advanced Topics in Systems (3 cr)

This course covers selected emerging and advanced topics in Systems. Topics may include: system programming, distributed systems, peer-to-peer systems, clustered systems, distributed file systems, replicated systems, content distribution systems, fault-tolerant systems, multimedia systems, real-time systems, virtualized systems etc. 


  • Advanced Topics in Data Science (3 cr)

This course examines selected emerging and advanced topics in Data Science. Topics may include: big data, data visualization techniques, data mining, statistical modeling and prediction, emerging data analysis techniques. 


  • Advanced Topics in Artificial Intelligence (3 cr)

This course examines selected emerging and advanced topics in Artificial Intelligence. Topics may include: searching strategies, constraint satisfaction, game playing, knowledge representation and reasoning, machine learning, applications to robotics. 


  • Advanced General Topics in Computer Science (3 cr)

This course covers selected emerging and advanced topics in Computer Science. Topics may include: programming, systems, software engineering, human computer interaction, algorithms, artificial intelligence, data science, robotics.

Founded in 1996, Vidzeme University of Applied Sciences (ViA) acquired in 2001 the status of State University.

The university offers flexible and high-quality study programs that balance theory and practice.

Vidzeme University of Applied Sciences (ViA) is a state higher education institution, which offers 16 study programmes at the Faculty of Society and Science and the Faculty of Engineering. In 2018, ViA celebrated the completion of its 22th academic year.

ViA is located in Valmeria, with a population 25,000 inhabitants. The city has plenty of green areas and the river 'Gauja' runs through Valmeria.

Vidzeme University of Applied Sciences works in collaboration with EkoTekNord, Businet, ATLAS, Microsoft Academy and IEEE Computer Society and has some facilities like a virtual reality and augmented reality laboratory , a computer network laboratory, a mobile technology laboratory as well as a Cybersecurity laboratory.

More than one-third of Latvia’s population lives and works in the capital city of Riga, the political, economic and cultural centre of the country.

Located by the Baltic Sea, Latvia boasts a 500-kilometre long coastline of beautiful beaches: gentle, white and sandy, as well as savage and rocky.

Latvia is in the top 10 countries with the fastest internet speeds in the world and Rīga has been named Europe’s capital of free WiFi.

Valmiera is the largest city in the historical Vidzeme region (one of the four historical territories in Latvia, in the north-east of Latvia), population is about 25 000. Even though the city is very small in European scale, it is rather active in cultural, sports, business and other areas.

Valmiera is situated 100 kilometres from the capital city of Latvia - Rīga, 120 kilometres from Tartu, Estonia. Through Valmiera meanders the picturesque River Gauja separating the city into two.

Valmiera is developing as a business and administrative center by investing in the development of culture, arts and sports. Our city motto is: Valmiera thinks and creates. The dominating economic branches in Valmiera are the food industry (milk, meat, and grain), fiberglass production, metalworking, wood processing and furniture production.

You must obtain 30 ECTS credits per semester, i.e 60 ECTS credits over the year.


Plan to arrive mid-august. The courses of the first semester takes place from the beginning of September to the end of January. The 2nd semester from the beginning of February to the end of June. You can find the academic calendar here https://va.lv/en/study-here/study-guide


The courses are taught in English.

The list of available courses can be found here.

You have to take the course of Latvian Language and Culture (3 ECTS). Please find below the courses you can attend:

Fall semester:​


Virtual reality and 3D modelling /6 ECTS:The aim of this course is to give a view about virtual and complementary reality technologies, their current topics and research. In addition, information will be provided on the platforms and projects for the development of these technologies and their relevance and development at the level of Latvia and the world. The course will provide a high level of knowledge and skills on the concepts of three-dimensional modelling, as well as higher-level modelling techniques. In addition, knowledge is provided in the design and creation of visual effects and their combination with real images and video footage, as well as the basic knowledge of scripting in Blender using Python programming language.

In this course, students will be familiarized with the basis of modelling, texturing, animating and other workflows. The course lessons will focus on the correct understanding of concepts and their application in different contexts, developing efficient models for various purposes, such as the development of computer games.

Project Work / 6 ECTS: The goal of the Project work is to show the application of the acquired theoretical knowledge and practical skills in development of a particular IT project and, if possible, also its implementation, as well as to develop the skills of research and analysis of the problem in correlations. It is accomplishment of several specified tasks with a pre-supposed result, that proves a profound acquisition of specific methods used in a sub-branch of IT or Engineering, skill of fixing the data, carrying out a comprehensive analysis, as well as practical skills in job performance. Content requirements ir to compile and design the paper according to the stages of its development or to strengthen the skill of executing a paper (research), ability of comprehensive analysis of the initial data; skills of working in a group of students or a scientific collective. To get acquainted with the principles of good research practice in a specific working branch. Topics can be selected from the themes offered by faculty lecturers (some of which might have been implemented in cooperation with Horizon or other scientific or applicable projects) or from the IT field chosen by the students themselves.

Modeling and formal specification / 3 ECTS : The course introduces students to modelling approaches used in varied context. Methodology and tools are provided so that students can practically model an organization. An overview of systems specification, systems analysis and simulation modelling is provided. Students will learn to evaluate and assess models and their results. Course content: Introduction to and concepts of modelling and formal specification; Overview of 4EM. Goals model; 4EM – business rules model; 4EM – concepts model; 4EM – business process model; 4EM – actors and resources model; 4EM – remaining issues and test; Simulation modelling. Agent-based modelling (Netlogo); Simulation modelling. Discrete-event-based modelling (Anylogic); Simulation modelling. System dynamics modelling (Anylogic); 4EM – analysis of test results; Evaluation of models, their quality; Other approaches to modelling.

VR/AR innovations and actuality in various industries / 3 ECTS : The aim of this course is to give practical and theoretical knowledge in virtual and augmented reality technologies innovations and actuality in various industries. In frames of this course students are introduced with successful use cases and their stories from real companies as well as with concepts and definitions of virtual and augmented reality, and fundamental approach for immersion and interaction. During practical demonstrations students will get opportunity to experience and understand technologies influence and benefits for museums, marketing, medicine, architecture etc. During practical demonstrations students will get opportunity to experience and understand visual interfaces, fixed support and wearable interfaces, and interfaces for interaction, tracking sensors, controllers and motion simulators. As a result, students prepare and present their chosen idea.

Programming advanced 3D graphics / 3 ECTS :The aim of this course is to give students knowledge about 3D graphics, which is one of data visualisation and virtual and augmented reality elements. During the course students will acquire knowledge about 3D graphics elements, such as creation and operation of 3D objects and their parameters, light, shading and texture. Object animation will be acquired using programming language and popular plugins such as three.js and others.

Course content: Introduction in 3D graphics; Explanation of 3D graphics terminology; 3D object creation principles and their parameter usage; View of 3D graphics elements – shading, texture, shapes and creation principles; 3D graphics element customization for development environment; Review of different 3D graphics tools; 3D graphic in World Wide Web; Review of usage and functionality of HTML5 Canvas; Test for theory and practical skills testing; Overview of HTML5 Canvas functions and usage; 3D graphic in World Wide Web; Three.js plugin usage; 3D graphics usage cases, real examples and overview; 3D graphic in World Wide Web; Three.js plugin usage; 3D graphics usage cases, real examples and overview.

Introduction to propaganda and influential communication / 3 ECTS :The aim of the course is to develop an in-depth understanding of the effectiveness of propaganda and influence, the development of technology at various stages of history. Insights into propaganda research approaches until the First world war, propaganda of modern times, propaganda and transmedia storytelling in the 21st century. As a result, students know and understand elements of an influential message, propaganda message, are able to apply appropriate techniques for recognizing propaganda and are able to analyze, evaluate, distinguish the propaganda message, influence the message.

Mobile technology solutions / 3 ECTS :The aim of this course is to provide theoretical and practical knowledge about current mobile technology solutions, including to gain insight about mobile application development environments, concepts, and particular development ways. By performing practical assignments students will have an opportunity to improve their practical skill in area of mobile technology solutions development. There is work done in small groups within the course. The study course is the preparatory step to enhance practical skills in development of mobile solutions and by combining them with VR/AR and other solutions to provide the foundation for multidisciplinary solutions development.

Data mining / 3 ECTS: The aim of the study course is to provide theoretical and practical knowledge of modern data mining solutions, including knowledge of application fields, concepts, concrete development techniques. Students have the opportunity to improve their practical skills in developing data mining solutions through practical work. During the course work is done in small groups. The study course is a preparatory stage to develop practical skills in the development of data mining solutions and combine them with cyber security and other skills acquired in other courses as a basis for interdisciplinary solutions.

Spring semester:


Geoinformation Systems/ 3 ECTS :The aim of this module is to introduce GIS used for different purposes in the large and middle size organizations up to individuals privately. It will present a number of technical and software solutions, which can be used to design, implement and use effective GIS environment. The course must give the skills necessary for using of technology (GIS) in the local networks, Internet as well as standalone PCs and mobile devices. At the end of the module, successful candidates should be able to: Explain how the GIS work, what components are needed; Demonstrate a detailed understanding of databases and cartography software links between graphical vector data and attribute databases; Show competence in the use of cartographical and attribute data available from data keepers in Latvia and worldwide; Demonstrate skills in use of mobile technologies; Compare and contrast the different types of data and systems, and select the most appropriate solutions to use in various circumstances.

Development of advanced 3D interactive environments / 3ECTS : Course objective is to give a general view into a three-dimensional environment development cycle and its basic principles and theoretical and practical knowledge in development of virtual and augmented reality systems. Course Contents: Intro in Unity and 3D engines; Unity hierarchy entities and their components; Visualisation; Perspective and orthographic camera projections; Physics; Keyframe animations; Animation controllers; Inverse kinematics; Motion capture; Unity application programming interface (API); Transformation mathematics; Coroutines; Interpolations and extrapolations; Unity user interface system; Optimisation; Surface shaders; Vert/Frag shaders; Virtual reality; Linear and gamma color spaces; Rendering techniques; Postprocessing effects; Augmented reality; Computer vision; Image recognition and tracking; Facial recognition; Object recognition and tracking; Motion tracking; Environmental understanding; Environmental light estimation.

Network, mobile, and cloud security / 3ECTS :The aim of the course is to get to know the best practices, tools and techniques to ensure the security of information resources using different ICT infrastructure.

Course content: Cloud services concepts, models, service types, infrastructure, Cloud services programming paradigm (MapReduce, BigTable, Hadoop), Cloud services quality, availability, performance, and security requirements, Introduction to mobile application security, Android, IOS security models, Mobile VoIP communications security. Learning Outcomes - students have an understanding of data management through cloud services, virtual infrastructure; students are able to find, pool and exploit the benefits of managing cloud-services and mobile services; students are able to evaluate, analyze, information security risks in cloud-service and mobile service management.

Information security risk management / 3ECTS :The course aims to increase students' awareness of information security risks in organizations, cyber-attacks and their protection measures.

Course Contents: risk management terminology in the context of cybersecurity, risk management lifecycle, quantitative and qualitative analysis, information analysis methods, information security risk monitoring methods, tools, metrics, information security risk treatment plan, implementation tactics. Learning Outcomes - students have in-deep knowledge of information security risks of the organization, students are able to apply appropriate methods, protection measures, security controls to implement information security system, students are able to analyze, evaluate the organization's information security risks, vulnerabilities, weaknesses and provide recommendations for their elimination.

Information systems audit and security / 3ECTS : The aim of the course is to develop an in-depth understanding of information security standards, good practice in conducting information system audits.

Course Contents: standards and good practices for conducting information system audit, information security responsibility, internal control objectives, ISO 27001 system design, appropriate auditing, monitoring procedures, outsourcing risks and security monitoring. Learning Outcomes: students know and understand the impact of organizational information security risks, security incident handling procedures, students are able to apply appropriate methods, safeguards, security controls to implement information security, students are able to analyze, evaluate, and evaluate the information security risks, vulnerabilities, vulnerabilities of the organization.

Data protection and security / 6 ECTS :The aim of the course is to provide an understanding of data protection and security in today's data transmission networks. Acquire knowledge and skills to maintain network security within a single organization.

Course Contents: information systems risk analysis, information protection, threats and vulnerabilities, types of attacks, cryptography, mixing functions, certificates and their management, web server, FTP and directory service protection, email security, wireless network protection, firewall, network perimeter. Learning outcomes: Course students gain knowledge of access control, authentication and auditing; after the course students are able to assess the system threats and vulnerabilities, distinguish between types of attacks and find the most appropriate means of protection for each; high emphasis is placed on cryptography, resulting in symmetric, asymmetric encryption algorithms, mixing functions, electronic signatures and certificate management; as a result, students are able to protect e-mail, http, servers, wireless networks and other popular technologies nowadays.

Innovations and project management / 3ECTS :The aim of this course is to give practical and theoretical knowledge in the latest tendencies in innovations and implementation. In frames of this course are introduced with innovation management methods, evaluate related risks. During practical workshops and independent tasks, students are given the opportunity to understand the process from creation of idea to business plan.

Course contents: innovation and project concept; creation of innovation and implementation steps, critical evaluation of innovation, proof of concept; innovation project team, innovation project implementation plan; innovation management tools; knowledge and technology transfer in innovation process; support attraction in innovation process - accelerators, business incubators, technology transfer centers, technology centers and parks, competency centers; business plan - problems, target customer, market, competitors, risk analysis; financing options and attraction; development of support attraction application; pitching and networking.

Project Work / 6 ECTS: The goal of the Project work is to show the application of the acquired theoretical knowledge and practical skills in development of a particular IT project and, if possible, also its implementation, as well as to develop the skills of research and analysis of the problem in correlations. It is accomplishment of several specified tasks with a pre-supposed result, that proves a profound acquisition of specific methods used in a sub-branch of IT or Engineering, skill of fixing the data, carrying out a comprehensive analysis, as well as practical skills in job performance. Content requirements ir to compile and design the paper according to the stages of its development or to strengthen the skill of executing a paper (research), ability of comprehensive analysis of the initial data; skills of working in a group of students or a scientific collective. To get acquainted with the principles of good research practice in a specific working branch. Topics can be selected from the themes offered by faculty lecturers (some of which might have been implemented in cooperation with Horizon or other scientific or applicable projects) or from the IT field chosen by the students themselves.


We remind you that attendance is compulsory, otherwise you can be expelled from the university.

The list of courses is given for information only. It can change from one year to the next. If a course is not available when you arrive on site, EPITECH can not be held responsible.

Some courses may require knowledge of mathematics.


Course Selection

  • The Safety in Electrical Engineering course is compulsory (course code begins with 410)

Course Format and Attendance

  • Each course is divided into two parts: a lecture part and a seminar part
  • Attendance of the seminar part is compulsory
  • All courses are face-to-face


Course Structure and Assessment

  • Teaching is fairly theoretical, with an obligation to read reference books
  • There is a practical part involving exercises and practicals

TOEFL 79 or TOEIC 785 or IELTS 6.5 or 127 on the Duolingo test

Wayne State University is a public research institution located in the heart of the historic and cultural center of Detroit, Michigan. It is one of the 100 largest American universities with its 822,000m² campus that can accommodate nearly 28,000 students. In recent years, the university has particularly focused its efforts on the development of its research and technology park.

Its College of Engineering offers a range of disciplines in engineering, including in several leading research areas in which faculty members focus on teamwork – alternative energy technology, automotive engineering, environmental infrastructure, transport engineering, materials engineering, nanotechnology and sustainable engineering, etc.

  • Immunization form to be completed by a doctor or by you but with a copy of your health record
  • Tuberculosis assessment certificate to be filled out by a doctor
  • Visa application form (J-1 Form DS-2019 Request)

This information is subject to change by the partner university. They will provide you with the most current information upon your acceptance.


To be given to Epitech bachelor campus administration to reenroll for the Tech4 (in April/May):

  • The addendum to the contract.
  • EPITECH re-registration dossier.


2. Visa (more information here)

You can find all the detailed information on the US government website or the Embassy of the US in Paris website. You can check the deadlines for obtaining an appointment here.


1/Admission letter and I-20 form

Once you are admitted by the host university, WSU will send you your acceptance letter for your visa. Please check the information on I-20 carefully and sign the document.


2/Pay the SEVIS fees

You must then pay the SEVIS I-901 fees online (here). Make sure you print the receipts. The fees for students are $350.


3/Complete the DS-160 form

Complete DS-160 form and upload an ID photo meeting the following requirements. Print the application form confirmation page to bring to your interview.

You will have to pay a visa application fee (non refundable) before your interview of $185 (more information here).


4/Schedule an appointment at the consulate

For people in France, you need to make an appointment for your interview at the US Consulate. Plan to travel to Paris for it.

If you live in another country, check the different consulate/embassy.


During your interview at the consulate, you must:

  • have the necessary supporting documents to prove that you qualify for the category of visa that you request--document relating to your current studies and its relationship to the studies you wish to pursue in the United States: academic transcript, various certificates, SAT or TOEFL test scores, diplomas, etc.
  • demonstrate, with supporting evidence, to the consular officer that you have solid family, social and financial ties to France and that you intend to return there once your residence permit has expired.
  • prove that you have the financial means necessary to finance your studies and live in good conditions in the United States for the first 12 months. Any document proving your family or relational ties with any person funding your studies, as well as bank statements, tax notices thereof.

Please note that the visa gives you the right to work 20 hours on campus.



3.Insurance and Health (more information here and here)

Health insurance is mandatory. All J-1 international students and scholars whose DS-2019 was issued by Wayne State University are required to enroll in the Wayne State University Student/Scholar Health Insurance (IHI) plan administered by AIG.


The student should not purchase health insurance in his/her home country because, in most instances, it will not meet the Wayne State University Health Insurance Standards, which are compliant with the US Federal Health Care Reform Law known as the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (PPACA).


The U.S. Department of State regulations (22 C.F.R 62.14) requires all J exchange visitors to have health insurance for the entire duration of their DS-2019. Any J-1 exchange visitor who willfully or negligently does not purchase health insurance for themselves and/or their family will be terminated from the WSU Exchange Visitor Program.


It'll cost you about 2500$ a year. For more information on the costs, click here.


In order to be fully covered for medical care, we recommend that you take out international insurance as well. It is imperative that you take out insurance that will cover you for your medical and hospital expenses, repatriation and accompanied by civil liability. International insurance must cover the entire period of your studies in the country. Insurance costs are the responsibility of each student. To take out international insurance, the market is quite open. Please click here for more information.


In addition, Tuberculosis (TB) testing is required for all international students. TB testing must be done within 30 days of arrival to the United States. 

For more information, you can consult the country’s health file at: https://www.pasteur.fr/fr/centre-medical/preparer-son-voyage/etats-unis

Note: It is advisable to register on the French register established outside France and to report to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs via the Ariane platform: https://pastel.diplomatie.gouv.fr/fildariane/dyn/public/login.html.


4. Prepare your arrival

The university gives advice for international students here.

For advice to travelers issued by the Ministry of Europe and Foreign Affairs on the host country, click here.

You can inform the university of your arrival date and your flight number so that they can arrange a pick-up at the airport. For this service, the partner university requests $70 per vehicle but students can share the costs if they are several sharing the pick-up vehicle.

Once there, you will have to pay $50 in SEVIS fees also to the partner university.

Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University (XJTLU)

Xi’an Jiaotong-Liverpool University (XJTLU) is a unique Higher Education institution located in Suzhou, Jiangsu Province, China.

It is the largest international collaborative university in China, established in 2006 by its parent institutions, the University of Liverpool (UK) and Xi’an Jiaotong University (China).

XJTLU enrolls Chinese students through the ‘’Gaokao’’ national examination system (tier 1 students) and international students through independent admissions.

XJTLU is situated on a purpose built campus in the Dushu Lake Higher Education Town, at the heart of one of Asia’s research and innovation hubs.
